steps.tx: An **achondroplasia** is the most common non-lethal chondrodysplasia, serving as the primary cause of disproportionate short-limbed dwarfism. It is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance, although over eighty percent of cases arise as spontaneous de novo mutations linked to advanced paternal age. The condition results from a point mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene on chromosome 4p16.
steps.say: Achondroplasia is the most common cause of short-limbed dwarfism. It is autosomal dominant with complete penetrance, but over eighty percent of cases are new spontaneous mutations linked to older father age. It is caused by a specific point mutation in the FGFR3 gene on chromosome four.

vis.alt: Skeletal diagram and clinical illustration of achondroplasia showing rhizomelic limb shortening and trident hand.
vis.caption: Characteristic rhizomelic micromelia and craniofacial features in achondroplasia.

steps.tx: The genetic mutation causes constitutive **gain-of-function** of the FGFR3 tyrosine kinase receptor. Because normal FGFR3 signaling acts as a physiological negative regulator of endochondral ossification, unconstrained activation severely suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy within long bone physis zones. Consequently, endochondral bone formation is profoundly retarded, whereas intramembranous and periosteal ossification proceed normally, creating short, stout cylindrical bones.
steps.say: The mutation causes a gain-of-function that makes the FGFR3 receptor constantly active. Because FGFR3 normally tells growth plates to slow down, constant activation shuts down chondrocyte proliferation. This halts endochondral bone lengthening while periosteal bone growth continues unimpeded, producing short, thick bones.

left.title: Endochondral Ossification Defect
points: Affects long tubular bones and skull base

right.title: Intramembranous Sparing
points: Normal trunk length and vertebral diameter

steps.tx: Clinical inspection reveals classic **rhizomelic micromelia**, where proximal limb segments (femur and humerus) are disproportionately shorter than middle and distal segments. Craniofacial features include macrocephaly with prominent frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia with a depressed nasal bridge. Hand examination demonstrates a trident hand, defined by short, broad, equal-length fingers with persistent divergence between the third and fourth digits.
steps.say: Look for rhizomelic micromelia, meaning the thighs and upper arms are disproportionately short compared to forearms and shins. The head is large with a bulging forehead and flattened nasal bridge. The fingers are short, stubby, and diverge between the middle and ring fingers, forming the classic trident hand.

vis.title: Phenotypic Characteristics of Achondroplasia
rows: Impaired proximal tubular growth plate kinetics
Short metacarpals with divergent fascial tethers
Normal membranous vault with stunted skull base
Fixed flexion deformity of hip joints

steps.tx: Radiographs demonstrate distinctive spinal and pelvic anomalies. The pathognomonic spinal hallmark is progressive **caudal interpedicular narrowing**, where the interpedicular distance decreases progressively from L1 down to L5, reversing normal widening. Pelvic views reveal squared iliac wings (tombstone appearance), flat horizontal acetabular roofs, and a narrow, champagne-glass shaped pelvic inlet, predisposing women to mandatory caesarean delivery.
steps.say: On spine X-rays, look at the distance between pedicles from L1 to L5. Instead of widening as it travels downward, the spinal canal gets progressively narrower. On pelvic films, the ilia look square like tombstones, the acetabular roofs are flat, and the pelvic opening is shaped like a champagne glass.

vis.title: Radiographic Hallmarks in Achondroplasia
rows: Normal spine widens progressively L1 to L5
Tombstone iliac wings and flat acetabular roof
Normal flared iliac wings and oblique roof

steps.tx: The most serious neurological complications stem from **foramen magnum stenosis**, predisposing infants to cervicomedullary cord compression, central sleep apnea, and sudden infant death. In adulthood, severe lumbar spinal stenosis manifests as neurogenic claudication. Somatropin and vosoritide (a C-type natriuretic peptide analogue that antagonizes downstream FGFR3 signaling) represent targeted medical therapies, while suboccipital decompression treats cervicomedullary impingement.
steps.say: The most dangerous complication in infants is stenosis of the foramen magnum. The narrow opening compresses the brainstem, causing central sleep apnea and sudden infant death. In adults, spinal canal narrowing causes neurogenic claudication. Vosoritide is an exciting new drug that blocks FGFR3 signaling, helping children grow taller.

right.title: Adult Lumbar Canal Stenosis
points: Congenital short pedicles plus facet hypertrophy
Relieved by spinal flexion and sitting

quiz.q: What is the genetic mechanism underlying achondroplasia?
options: Constitutive gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene
Loss-of-function deletion in the COL1A1 gene
Inactivating mutation in the parathyroid hormone receptor
quiz.explain: Achondroplasia is caused by a heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 (most commonly G380R), which excessively inhibits chondrocyte proliferation during endochondral ossification.

quiz.q: What pathognomonic radiographic sign is seen in the lumbar spine on anteroposterior views in achondroplasia?
options: Progressive caudal narrowing of interpedicular distance from L1 to L5
Progressive widening of the interpedicular distance from L1 to L5
Complete fusion of the posterior neural arches across all levels
Universal presence of lumbar hemivertebrae with scoliosis
quiz.explain: In achondroplasia, the lumbar interpedicular distance progressively narrows from L1 down to L5 (caudal narrowing), reversing the normal anatomical widening pattern.
